title: Distributed Training Across GPUs
intro: One GPU isn't enough for the new model, so training has to spread across four on this node, and later across nodes. Distributed training fails in its own ways: one process hangs the rest, GPUs wait on each other, and the effective batch size changes without anyone deciding it should.

steps.prompt: Check how the GPUs are connected to each other and to the CPUs.
steps.fake_output:
GPU0  GPU1  GPU2  GPU3  CPU Affinity  NUMA Affinity
GPU0     X    NV4   SYS   SYS   0-31          0
GPU1    NV4    X    SYS   SYS   0-31          0
GPU2    SYS   SYS    X    NV4   32-63         1
GPU3    SYS   SYS   NV4    X    32-63         1
steps.explanation: GPUs 0-1 and 2-3 are each linked by NVLink (NV4); across the pairs they go through the system bus (SYS).
steps.why: Training constantly passes gradients between GPUs, so the slowest link sets the pace. NVLink is far faster than going through PCIe and the CPU. Knowing the topology explains why 4 GPUs sometimes give much less than a 4x speed-up.

steps.prompt: Launch train.py on all 4 GPUs of this node with PyTorch's distributed launcher.
steps.fake_output:
[rank 0] using cuda:0  [rank 1] using cuda:1  [rank 2] using cuda:2  [rank 3] using cuda:3
epoch 0 step 100  loss 2.412  1,840 samples/s
steps.explanation: Four processes, one per GPU, training one model together.
steps.why: torchrun starts one process per GPU and sets up their ranks; the script wraps the model in DistributedDataParallel. Each process sees a different slice of the data per step. If one process crashes, torchrun stops the rest, which is better than three processes waiting for ever on the fourth.

steps.prompt:
Each GPU now processes a batch of 64, so the effective batch size is 256. If you leave the learning rate at its single-GPU value, what's the usual consequence and fix?
  a) Nothing changes
  b) Training is slower to converge per sample; scale the learning rate up roughly in proportion to the batch size, with a warm-up
  c) Training crashes with out-of-memory
  d) The model becomes more accurate automatically
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
1 GPU:  batch 64,  lr 0.001
4 GPUs: batch 256, lr 0.004 (linear scaling rule), ramped up over the first few hundred steps
steps.hint: Four times the batch means four times fewer weight updates per epoch.
steps.explanation: Scale the learning rate with the batch size, and warm it up.
steps.why: Going distributed silently changes the training recipe: bigger batches mean fewer, smoother updates. The linear scaling rule with a warm-up is the standard starting point. Results that 'got worse after we added GPUs' are very often this, not a bug.

steps.prompt: A multi-node run hangs at start-up with no error. Rerun it with NCCL's debug output turned on to see where the GPUs fail to connect.
steps.fake_output:
NCCL INFO NET/Socket : Using [0]eth0:10.0.5.11<0> [1]docker0:172.17.0.1<0>
NCCL INFO NET/Socket : selected interface docker0
NCCL WARN Connect to 172.17.0.1<49152> failed : Connection timed out
steps.explanation: NCCL picked the docker0 bridge interface, which other nodes can't reach.
steps.why: NCCL is the library GPUs use to talk to each other, and a silent hang at start-up is almost always it choosing the wrong network interface or being blocked by a firewall. NCCL_DEBUG=INFO shows the choice; NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0 fixes it. Without the debug flag this looks like a frozen job with nothing to go on.

steps.prompt: On Kubernetes, distributed jobs are run by the Kubeflow Training Operator. Check the status of PyTorch jobs in the namespace ml.
steps.fake_output:
NAME            STATE     AGE
resnet-ddp-01   Running   14m
bert-ft-07      Failed    2h
steps.explanation: One job is running, and one failed.
steps.why: A PyTorchJob creates a master pod and worker pods and wires up their addresses, replacing hand-built launch scripts. For jobs that run for days, the essentials are checkpointing (so a lost node costs minutes, not days) and all-or-nothing scheduling (so a job that needs 8 GPUs doesn't start with 5 and wait).
